transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2025-09-25
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 56 minutes
Attendees: Alex Martinez (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Daniel Park (Nimbus CTO), Leah Kim (Nimbus ML Eng), Omar Ruiz (Nimbus Infra)

Summary (auto): quick deep dive on tool/function-calling in JSON mode and perf implications; discuss KV cache, batching, quantization, and private/VPC performance tradeoffs; agree next steps to run benchmarks and share prompts/docs.

Topics (auto): runtime perf, constrained decoding/JSON mode, KV cache behavior, batching strategy, quantization impact, private/VPC networking constraints

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: hey everyone thanks for joining, uh I think we have about an hour, we'll go through priya's perf notes and then dig into your constraints.
[00:12] Daniel: cool thanks alex, um we really wanna understand the overhead of json mode and tool calling; our regulators will require structured outputs and we need low tail latency for patient-facing flows.
[00:23] Priya: yeah totally, and quick note, i'll be demoing some traces from our runtime, there might be small transcript typos, forgive me, i recorded some logs.
[00:30] Leah: also high level we're using 4k context right now, but we expect some sessions to hit 8k, and most outputs are structured small JSONs, ~60-200 tokens.
[00:44] Omar: infra side, we run on mixed gpus, mainly A10G and some A100s on prem, and if we go private we need VPC peering and strict egress rules.
[00:56] Priya: ok great, starting with the big picture: tool-calling and constrained decoding (json mode) introduce overhead primarily in two places - the extra token-level constraints and the post-processing validation, plus any reroll or constrained beam search. in our runtime we try to convert constraints into decoding masks where possible to avoid sampling wasted tokens.
[01:20] Daniel: can you quantify that? like, what is the typical increase in per-token latency?
[01:24] Priya: rough ballpark from our internal benches: naive constrained decoding (off-the-shelf plugin) added 20-30% token latency; with our optimized masked decode it's more like 5-12% depending on sequence length and model. for short 60-200 token responses it's closer to the high end of that range because setup/overhead is proportionally bigger.
[01:46] Alex: note that we also use KV cache aggressively; that reduces decode compute for subsequent tokens but constrained decoding still needs per-step mask application, which is cheap but non-zero.
[01:58] Leah: how does KV cache interact with json mode? any issues with structured outputs where previous tokens change mask decisions?
[02:06] Priya: good question. KV cache stores key/value states so you don't re-run the prefix, but since constrained decoding only affects logits during sampling, it doesn't invalidate KV cache. the trick is when you do partial re-rolls or editing in the middle — then you may need to evict or recompute the later KV entries. for normal prefix->generate flows it's fine.
[02:29] Omar: we sometimes do streaming where the UI validates json incrementally; does that break caching?
[02:34] Priya: streaming plus incremental validation can cause back-and-forth. streaming tokens still hit cache; validation at the client doesn't change server decode state. if you rely on server-side incremental constrained re-synthesis (like forcing certain keys after seeing partial output), then you'll trigger more compute.
[02:51] Daniel: ok makes sense. what about batching? we can't add latency for each user session but want throughput for cost reasons.
[02:58] Priya: batching is our primary cost lever. for JSON-mode constrained outputs, batching still helps but you need to align sequences or do dynamic batching. our runtime uses continuous batching and per-request time budgets to avoid head-of-line blocking. for JSON outputs with small responses, we tend to use micro-batches that give good GPU utilization and keep p50 latency low.
[03:21] Alex: an important point — for hosted vs dedicated vs private, the batching policies differ. hosted can do larger multi-tenant batch windows; dedicated reserved pools are usually customer-isolated so batch sizes depend on committed qps. private on-prem depends on your infra and queueing config.
[03:39] Leah: if we commit to dedicated, what latency should we expect for 200-token JSON outputs on A10G vs A100?
[03:45] Priya: A100 with fp16 is fastest — p50 single-request decode for 200 tokens with KV warm is around 120-160ms outside of constrained decode overhead. on A10G it's closer to 220-300ms. constrained json mode adds the 5-12% we mentioned, so you should budget accordingly. these are rough and vary with model and sequence distribution.
[04:12] Omar: and quantization — we are interested in int8 for cost reduction. does quantization blow up constrained decode errors or make structured outputs less reliable?
[04:20] Priya: quantization like 8-bit (INT8) can introduce small distribution shifts. for many tasks it is fine but for strict JSON schema adherence you might see more off-by-one tokens or more need for post-validators. we recommend unit tests: run the eval set and measure schema pass rate. our Redwood Optimize team also suggests mixing fp16 for the head layers and int8 for the rest, or per-layer quantization to minimize hallucination in constrained scenarios.
[04:47] Daniel: is that something priya can run in the benchmark? we want to compare fp16 vs int8 for JSON pass rates and latency.
[04:52] Priya: yes, we'll include fp16, int8, and a hybrid config in the bench runs.
[04:57] Alex: note on private installs: if you use customer-managed KMS/HSM for key operations, some cryptographic ops may slightly affect cold-start times for TLS/KMS handshakes, but once warmed it's minimal. also network egress to control plane is tiny unless you're streaming heavy telemetry.
[05:18] Omar: about VPC peering — we need to ensure traffic stays internal, and we need to run the private control plane. how intrusive is the on-prem package?
[05:25] Priya: on-prem package is containerized and supports air-gapped deployments. the main requirements are GPUs with supported drivers, a kubernetes cluster (we support k8s 1.24+), and a small set of ports for telemetry to the control plane if you choose managed control plane; for fully air-gapped we provide a bundle. we'll send the checklist.
[05:44] Leah: back to perf — can you walk through an example where constrained decoding fails and you need to reroll? what's the perf impact?
[05:50] Priya: sure — imagine you constrain for exact keys ordering in JSON. if the beam or sample produces an invalid token you either post-process and attempt repair (server-side repair costs another decode), or you trigger constrained resampling which increases latency by roughly another 50-200% for that request depending on whether you re-decode full sequence or just tail. we usually try to avoid full re-decodes by using stronger constraints and token masks.
[06:20] Alex: we also have a fallback policy — if JSON mode fails repeatedly we can return a partial payload + a validation error field so clients can decide. that trades strictness for latency.
[06:34] Daniel: okay, interesting. can we see the logs/traces you mentioned?
[06:38] Priya: yes i'll share an anonymized trace. quick pause while i pull the trace.
[07:02] Priya: sharing trace link in chat (note: link is internal); in the trace you can see the per-token time breakdown: kernel exec vs mask-apply vs token sampling. mask-apply is small but visible for short responses.
[07:18] Leah: the trace also shows a spike at 00:23 - what's that?
[07:22] Priya: that's a cache miss — a rare recompute after a partial edit. we instrument cache hit ratios and we'll show that in the bench.
[07:32] Omar: about KV cache size — does it grow with context length? any memory pressure we should plan for?
[07:37] Priya: yes KV cache grows linearly with context length and batch size. for 8k contexts you'll see significantly more memory use; some GPUs may need memory-saver configs like activation offloading or smaller batch sizes. we have autoscaling heuristics to avoid OOMs.
[07:56] Alex: note new features in runtime: smart KV compaction to drop early prefix KV when it's unlikely to be referenced (like long system prompts that don't impact later tokens) — helps memory but is heuristic.
[08:12] Daniel: interesting — any impact on security or determinism?
[08:15] Priya: compaction is transparent to user outputs; it's only safe when later tokens don't reference compressed keys. we validate heuristics in our tests but recommend caution if you require bit-for-bit reproducibility.
[08:28] Leah: circling back to batching — if we do low-latency interactive flows with 50-100ms target, can Redwood do micro-batching without hurting p99?
[08:36] Priya: yes micro-batching with continuous batching windows of ~5-20ms is common. that lets you hit good throughput with small latency overhead. p99 depends heavily on variability; for strict p99 SLOs we recommend reserved dedicated capacity to avoid noisy neighbor issues.
[08:52] Omar: is there a quantized kernel for int8 that supports masked decoding? some runtimes have gaps that force you back to fp16 for constrained mode.
[08:59] Priya: good callout — our runtime includes quantized kernels with masked decode support on recent GPUs. older or vendor drivers might not expose necessary ops. if you pick a quantized path and you need constrained masks, we'll validate kernel availability during onboarding and fallback to mixed precision if needed.
[09:20] Daniel: about throughput — if we run a batch of 32 short JSON requests, what's the expected tokens/sec?
[09:25] Priya: depends on GPU. example: on A100 with fp16 you might see ~15-25k tokens/sec for small responses; int8 improves cost per token and sometimes increases throughput to 18-30k depending on kernel. but remember constrained masks reduce effective tokens/sec a bit.
[09:44] Alex: i'll add a bench scenario: 32 concurrent sessions, avg output 120 tokens, 20% chance of reroll, compare fp16/int8/ hybrid, and hosted/dedicated/private.
[09:59] Leah: on the schema side, we plan to run strict validator and then a tolerant parser that can autocorrect small errors. how would you recommend we combine server-side and client-side validation?
[10:10] Priya: best practice: server-side strict validate to compute a pass/fail metric, but return a structure with both the emitted json and a normalized canonical form if parsed. then client-side can apply corrections or request a re-decode only when necessary. that reduces re-decode frequency.
[10:28] Daniel: any specific tips for prompt design to reduce constrained failure rate?
[10:32] Priya: yes. 1) include explicit schema examples in the system prompt, 2) canonicalize keys and small vocabulary where possible, 3) avoid free-form text in required fields, 4) encourage deterministic sampling (lower temperature) for structured outputs, and 5) for high reliability use small beams or constrained sampling plus post-validators.
[10:52] Omar: on the private networking side, if we host on-prem with persistent private control plane, can Redwood run all runtime GPUs locally and still get support for rollout/metrics?
[11:00] Alex: yes we support private control plane with local runtime; you can opt into telemetry exports (to a customer s3) and we still provide rollout orchestration via our management plane if you open a small control channel. full air-gapped mode removes that and we ship artifacts for local ops.
[11:16] Leah: how about model version pinning and canary for JSON-mode behavior changes? we need to avoid regressions.
[11:22] Priya: we do pinned model versions and canary rollouts by default. also Redwood Optimize can run evals (your prompts) across new model builds and report regression alerts (schema pass rate, latency changes, etc.). we tie that to automatic rollback policies.
[11:38] Daniel: perfect. one more question: we've seen some vendors drop into guided generation APIs rather than constrained decoding. does Redwood support tool-calls vs mask-based constrained? which is preferable?
[11:48] Priya: we support both. tool-calling (where model emits a function call signal and structured args) is often easier for downstream processing. constrained mask-based decoding is stricter but can be more expensive. often hybrid is best: prefer tool-calls for clear structured actions and masks when strict lexical format is required.
[12:07] Alex: also practical note: tool-calls can reduce post-processing because the model returns arguments as typed fields, which can be validated easier, but they require model support (some open models handle it better than others).
[12:20] Leah: so for our use-case (patient form autofill and triage decisions) we probably want strict json for critical fields and tool-call for actions, agreed?
[12:29] Daniel: yes agreed.
[12:31] Priya: ok we'll include a hybrid bench. next i'll outline the exact configs we'll run.
[12:36] Priya: Config A: Hosted multi-tenant, fp16, KV cache on, constrained mask decoding, micro-batch 8, 4k context.
[12:46] Priya: Config B: Dedicated reserved A100, fp16, KV cache on, constrained mask decoding, batch 32, 8k context.
[12:55] Priya: Config C: Private on-prem A10G, int8 quant, KV cache on, fallback mixed precision for masked ops, batch 16, 8k context.
[13:08] Priya: For each we'll measure: p50/p90/p99 latency, tokens/sec, schema pass rate, and re-decode frequency.
[13:19] Leah: sounds great. also include the hybrid fp16-int8 config.
[13:24] Priya: yep will do.
[13:27] Alex: any blockers from your side on getting sample prompts and infra details?
[13:31] Leah: we'll redact PHI and provide synthetic prompts, also share the expected JSON schema and a small eval harness.
[13:39] Omar: i'll confirm which gpus we can expose for benching and any networking constraints.
[13:44] Daniel: timeline — we want pilots in early october.
[13:48] Alex: we'll aim for bench results by 2025-10-02, then sync next week of 10/6.
[13:55] Priya: quick note on metrics export: we can send per-token traces and aggregated metrics to your S3 bucket or to the Redwood console if you prefer.
[14:05] Leah: S3 is fine, we'll share bucket details.
[14:09] Alex: wrapping up — any last concerns?
[14:12] Daniel: just curious about costs for int8 vs fp16 on dedicated — i assume int8 cheaper but still need to weigh pass rate.
[14:20] Priya: yes int8 reduces unit GPU cost but may increase validation failures; bench will quantify cost per successful schema.
[14:28] Omar: also please include memory footprints per config so we can assess OOM risk.
[14:33] Priya: noted.
[14:36] Alex: thanks all, we'll send the plan and schedule the follow-up.
[14:40] Daniel: thanks team.

[14:50] End of recording.
